author: A Robot
objectives: Identify and name the four chambers of the heart, the four heart valves, and the major vessels entering and leaving the heart.
Trace the path of blood through the heart's dual circulation, naming each chamber, valve, and vessel in order.
Distinguish the pulmonary circuit from the systemic circuit and explain why the right and left sides of the heart serve different circulatory functions.
Explain why the left ventricle has a substantially thicker myocardium than the right ventricle, relating wall thickness to systemic versus pulmonary pressure demands.
Describe how atrioventricular and semilunar valves prevent backflow and identify the structures each valve separates.

modules.moduleName: Scene 1: External Orientation and Major Vessels
modules.description: Students orient to a tabletop 3D heart model and identify the major vessels entering and leaving the heart before examining internal structures.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Orient the heart model anatomically by distinguishing anterior, superior, right, and left directions.
Identify the superior vena cava, inferior vena cava, pulmonary arteries, pulmonary veins, and aorta.
Relate vessel color-coding to oxygenation status while noting that pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood and pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood.
instructions: Place the heart model on a clear tabletop or floor surface with at least 1 meter of open space.
Use Next and Previous to step through the guided orientation.
Walk around the model if possible; labels will remain near the structures they identify.

components.text: Anterior view: apex points down and left
Major vessels
Anterior view: apex down and to patient's left

clips.changeMeaning: The external heart model is presented alone with an orientation label so students can establish anatomical direction before details are added.
clips.narration: Begin by orienting yourself to the heart. In this anterior view, the apex points inferiorly and toward the patient's left, while the broad base sits superiorly where the great vessels attach.

components.text:
Superior & Inferior Vena Cava
(systemic venous return)

clips.changeMeaning: Blue highlights appear over the superior and inferior vena cava to show the main systemic venous return pathways into the right atrium.
clips.narration: Deoxygenated blood returning from the systemic circuit enters the right atrium through two large veins: the superior vena cava from the head, neck, and upper limbs, and the inferior vena cava from the trunk and lower limbs.

components.text:
Pulmonary arteries
blue = deoxygenated to lungs

clips.changeMeaning: The pulmonary artery highlight is introduced while vena cava highlights remain visible, linking right-sided venous entry to pulmonary outflow.
clips.narration: From the right ventricle, deoxygenated blood leaves through the pulmonary trunk, which branches into the right and left pulmonary arteries. Unusually, these arteries carry deoxygenated blood to the lungs.

components.text:
Pulmonary veins and aorta
red = oxygenated blood

clips.changeMeaning: Red highlights reveal pulmonary venous return and aortic systemic outflow to contrast oxygenated pathways with deoxygenated pathways.
clips.narration: Oxygenated blood returns from the lungs through four pulmonary veins into the left atrium. It then exits the left ventricle through the aorta, the largest systemic artery.

modules.description: A cutaway model reveals the four chambers, four valves, and different myocardial wall thicknesses of the right and left ventricles.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify the right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, and left ventricle in a cutaway heart.
Locate the tricuspid, pulmonary, mitral, and aortic valves and state which structures each separates.
Compare right and left ventricular myocardium and relate wall thickness to pumping pressure.
instructions: Study the cutaway heart from the front; the patient’s right side appears on your left.
Follow each label as it appears, then compare valve positions and ventricular wall thickness.
Use the labels to rehearse chamber and valve names aloud before advancing.

components.text: Cutaway heart: chambers and valves
Patient's right side appears on your left

clips.changeMeaning: The cutaway heart appears with a general label, preparing students to map internal structures from an anterior view.
clips.narration: This cutaway exposes the four chambers. Remember that the anatomical right side of the heart is on your left as you face the model.

components.text:
Right atrium → Right ventricle
pulmonary pump

clips.changeMeaning: Blue chamber highlights mark the right atrium and right ventricle to connect right heart structures with deoxygenated blood flow.
clips.narration: The right atrium receives systemic venous blood from the venae cavae. Blood then passes into the right ventricle, which pumps it a short distance to the lungs.

components.text:
Left atrium → Left ventricle
systemic pump

clips.changeMeaning: Red chamber highlights identify the left atrium and left ventricle, contrasting oxygenated systemic-side chambers with right-side chambers.
clips.narration: The left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins. The left ventricle pumps blood into the systemic circuit through the aorta.

components.text:
AV valves: tricuspid and mitral
prevent backflow into atria

clips.changeMeaning: Atrioventricular valve rings appear between atria and ventricles, clarifying how tricuspid and mitral valves prevent atrial backflow.
clips.narration: The atrioventricular valves sit between atria and ventricles. The tricuspid valve separates the right atrium from the right ventricle. The mitral, or bicuspid, valve separates the left atrium from the left ventricle.

components.text:
Semilunar valves: pulmonary and aortic
prevent backflow into ventricles

clips.changeMeaning: Semilunar valve rings appear at the ventricular exits to distinguish outflow valves from atrioventricular valves.
clips.narration: The semilunar valves guard the ventricular outflow tracts. The pulmonary valve separates the right ventricle from the pulmonary trunk. The aortic valve separates the left ventricle from the aorta.

components.text: Thicker left ventricle = higher systemic pressure

clips.changeMeaning: A caliper callout appears at the left ventricular wall while the heart rotates slightly to emphasize the greater myocardial thickness.
clips.narration: Compare the ventricular walls. The left ventricular myocardium is substantially thicker because it must generate enough pressure to perfuse the entire systemic circuit. The right ventricle pumps only to the nearby lungs, so it operates at lower pressure.

modules.moduleName: Scene 3: Tracing Blood Flow Through Dual Circulation
modules.description: Animated colored blood cells trace the complete pathway through the right heart, pulmonary circuit, left heart, and systemic circuit.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Trace deoxygenated blood from the body through the right heart to the lungs in correct order.
Trace oxygenated blood from the lungs through the left heart to the systemic circuit in correct order.
Distinguish pulmonary circulation from systemic circulation using route, color, and destination.
instructions: Watch the moving blood markers and read the sequence label at each step.
Blue markers indicate relatively deoxygenated blood; red markers indicate oxygenated blood.
At the end, rehearse the entire pathway from venae cavae to aorta.

components.text: Blood flow pathway

Two loops in series:
Right heart → lungs → Left heart → body

clips.changeMeaning: The transparent heart, lungs, body icons, and initial blue blood marker establish the dual-loop circulation layout.
clips.narration: The heart drives two circuits in series. The right heart sends blood to the pulmonary circuit for gas exchange. The left heart sends blood to the systemic circuit to supply the body.

components.text: Body → SVC/IVC → Right atrium

clips.changeMeaning: The blue blood marker moves from the systemic body icon toward the right atrium, illustrating venous return through the venae cavae.
clips.narration: Start with deoxygenated blood returning from body tissues. It travels through systemic veins, then enters the right atrium by way of the superior and inferior vena cava.

components.text: Right atrium → Tricuspid valve → Right ventricle

clips.changeMeaning: The blue marker descends through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, emphasizing the first atrioventricular valve.
clips.narration: From the right atrium, blood passes through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle. When the ventricle contracts, this valve closes to prevent backflow into the atrium.

components.text: Right ventricle → Pulmonary valve → Pulmonary arteries → Lungs

clips.changeMeaning: The marker moves upward and outward to the lungs through the pulmonary valve and arteries, defining the pulmonary circuit outflow.
clips.narration: The right ventricle pumps blood through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk and pulmonary arteries. This is the pulmonary circuit: blood travels to the lungs to pick up oxygen.

components.text: Lungs → Pulmonary veins → Left atrium

clips.changeMeaning: The blue marker is replaced by a red marker that moves from the lungs to the left atrium, illustrating oxygenation and pulmonary venous return.
clips.narration: After gas exchange in the lungs, the blood is oxygenated. It returns to the left atrium through the pulmonary veins, which carry oxygenated blood.

components.text: Left atrium → Mitral valve → Left ventricle

clips.changeMeaning: The red marker descends through the mitral valve into the left ventricle, pairing oxygenated inflow with the left atrioventricular valve.
clips.narration: From the left atrium, oxygenated blood passes through the mitral, or bicuspid, valve into the left ventricle. This ventricle is the high-pressure systemic pump.

components.text: Left ventricle → Aortic valve → Aorta → Body

clips.changeMeaning: The red marker moves from the left ventricle to the systemic body icon through the aortic valve and aorta, completing the dual circulation loop.
clips.narration: Finally, the left ventricle pumps blood through the aortic valve into the aorta. From there, arteries distribute oxygenated blood throughout the systemic circuit.

components.text:
Full route:
Body → SVC/IVC → RA → Tricuspid → RV → Pulmonary valve → Pulmonary arteries → Lungs → Pulmonary veins → LA → Mitral → LV → Aortic valve → Aorta → Body

clips.changeMeaning: Both blood markers and a centered sequence label provide a final recap of the entire pathway for rehearsal and self-check.
clips.narration: Recap the pathway in order: body, venae cavae, right atrium, tricuspid valve, right ventricle, pulmonary valve, pulmonary arteries, lungs, pulmonary veins, left atrium, mitral valve, left ventricle, aortic valve, aorta, and body.

modules.moduleName: Scene 4: Valve Action During the Cardiac Cycle
modules.description: Students observe how atrioventricular and semilunar valves open and close to maintain one-way blood flow during filling and ejection.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Differentiate atrioventricular valve function from semilunar valve function during ventricular filling and systole.
Explain how valve closure prevents backflow into atria or ventricles.
Connect pressure changes during the cardiac cycle to the direction of valve movement.
instructions: Focus on the valve panels and moving pressure arrows.
Compare which valves are open during ventricular filling versus ventricular ejection.
Notice how backflow blockers appear when valves close.

components.text: Valve function in one-way flow
AV valves vs. semilunar valves

clips.changeMeaning: The valve-focused heart section appears with separate atrioventricular and semilunar valve models for a focused comparison.
clips.narration: Valves keep blood moving in one direction. Atrioventricular valves control flow from atria to ventricles, while semilunar valves control flow from ventricles into arteries.

components.text:
Filling: AV valves open
Semilunar valves closed

clips.changeMeaning: Downward filling arrows appear and AV leaflets open while semilunar leaflets close, showing passive ventricular filling.
clips.narration: During ventricular filling, atrial pressure is greater than ventricular pressure. The atrioventricular valves open, allowing blood to enter the ventricles. The semilunar valves remain closed.

components.text:
Systole: AV valves closed
Semilunar valves open

clips.changeMeaning: Ejection arrows appear and valve leaflet rotations reverse to show ventricular contraction opening semilunar valves and closing AV valves.
clips.narration: During ventricular systole, ventricular pressure rises. The atrioventricular valves close to stop blood from re-entering the atria, while the pulmonary and aortic semilunar valves open for ejection.

components.text:
Semilunar closure prevents
artery-to-ventricle backflow

clips.changeMeaning: Backflow stop symbols shift to the semilunar valve side, illustrating closure after ejection when arterial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure.
clips.narration: After ejection, ventricular pressure falls below arterial pressure. The aortic and pulmonary valves close, preventing blood in the aorta and pulmonary trunk from flowing backward into the ventricles.
